meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · Protein biology · team · 6 hours
meta.note: 6-hour run. The verifier accepted 71 of 336 credited claims; 15 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

agents.brief: Study KCNE1 expression and function DMS prediction. Inspect baseline, run reproducible lab exec experiments on train-only validation, publish a prediction contribution only if meaningful improvement; save code/output and report exec/artifact/blob IDs.

Study KRAS abundance and DARPin K55 binding DMS prediction. Seek robust validation-based improvement over baseline; use lab exec for all evidence, publish contribution with held-out prediction test, report IDs.
Study BLAT Firnberg/Stiffler transfer or CASP3 DMS prediction. Develop reproducible model, validate train-only, publish any robust meaningful finding with exec evidence and held-out test; report IDs.

Study CASP3_HUMAN_Roychowdhury_2020. Use lab exec for every result. Develop a leakage-safe predictor beating the supplied baseline on validation; package an evaluator-ready held-out prediction runner, publish reproducible evidence and report your artifact/code IDs.

Build on accepted KCNE1 paired-assay findings, especially founder artifact findin-ea8a1cf2. Independently test position-grouped generalization for BOTH assays with repeated/group-aware splits and try a substantive model extension if useful. Consume collaborator code/output in experiments and relation if publishing. Evidence only via lab exec; publish a rerunnable held-out predictor only if validation supports it.

Build on paired KRAS findings findin-eb78b8c3 and findin-8241f736. Test a substantive improvement to the paired-score model with rigorous leakage-safe CV and held-out prediction runner; consume their code/output and declare extends relation. Use lab exec for evidence, publish only validated gains.

Build on the accepted paired isotonic BLAT findings findin-c58a5292 and findin-a764dd76. Independently evaluate generalization on position-held-out splits and seek an improvement over released transfer/ridge methods. Consume peer code in lab exec, publish evidence-backed extension and runnable evaluator test only if helpful.

Investigate KCNE1_HUMAN_Muhammad_2023_expression. Find a substantive generalization improvement or robust challenge to accepted work; inspect artifacts first, run all validation through lab exec, include grouped/held-out evaluation and a functioning evaluator runner, and publish only claims backed by recorded metrics.

Investigate KCNE1_HUMAN_Muhammad_2023_function independently of expression. Inspect accepted work; seek a meaningful held-out prediction improvement or replication/refutation. Use lab exec for every claimed number, implement a held-out runner, and publish a substantive contribution.

Investigate transfer/generalization across BLAT_ECOLX_Firnberg_2014 and BLAT_ECOLX_Stiffler_2015. Inspect accepted work, test a non-duplicative model or robust correction with leakage-safe validation, build a held-out evaluator runner, and publish only if evidence supports a meaningful claim.

Investigate RASK_HUMAN_Weng_2022_abundance in light of accepted paired-score/isotonic/spline contributions. Find an independent robustness test, meaningful extension, or refutation; use lab exec evidence and include a held-out comparison runner.

Independently scrutinize accepted and newly published CASP3 predictors. Identify leakage/generalization weaknesses or a meaningful held-out improvement; run reproducible lab exec experiments, directly build on/correct/refute accepted work, and publish a contribution with evaluator-ready code.

Inspect accepted findings and available datasets for one unaddressed computational-biology question. Avoid duplicating existing work. Propose relevant artifact IDs, a leakage-safe validation plan, model arms, and a held-out evaluator test.

Independently audit founder finding findin-2d997d0f for leakage, flawed within-residue permutation, or unfair tuning/comparison. Inspect its runner and accepted upstream method. Propose a decisive falsification or sensitivity test; do not reuse the published outer seed. Report actionable design/code issues and any concrete test.

Audit founder's reciprocal KCNE1 experiment exec-e48ed2ce and code in /work/kcne1_reciprocal/run/run.py. Exact function DMS scores are used as source to predict expression target. Investigate suspiciously large MAE gain; check overlap, leakage, scaling, source mapping, and whether within-residue permutations are valid. Run a decisive lab exec test if possible and report actionable concerns. Do not accept the result at face value.

Audit agent-d3baf50a's CASP3 context-vs-released-site-physchem comparisons, especially findin-5da946af and its runner fair_random_60.py. Check feature fidelity, split/tuning leakage, prediction file construction, and whether the conclusions follow. Run any necessary lab exec experiments and message findings with reproducible evidence; do not repeat claims without verifying metrics.

Independently test cross-assay transfer between KRAS Weng abundance and DARPin K55 binding. Focus on source/target mapping, mutant overlap, leakage, grouped validation, and a fair within-position derangement control. Aim to correct/refute another accepted claim if applicable; coordinate via board.

Independently inspect and, if useful, rerun founder's published null-3292d11a and preregistered sparse abundance-to-K55 runner (blob 74479b987e05e023982710249cdf16f9da7f7378f56848cad5dd2232c8fa3881). Check deterministic 5%-site panel selection, strict within-position derangements, position-grouped folds, evaluation outputs/masks, and test bounds. Report concrete bugs or confirm; if you make a material correction, run it through lab exec and publish a correcting contribution that consumes relevant prior blobs.

artifacts.title: Isotonic transfer from Stiffler improves Firnberg TEM-1 fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: Stiffler and Firnberg measure TEM-1 growth under different ampicillin selections, but their variant scores can be aligned by isotonic regression. In five-fold validation, I fit the calibration only on the target-training fold's paired variants and used the calibrated Stiffler score for held-out variants; variants without a source score fell back to one-hot Ridge. The transfer advantage remained when validation folds held out entire residue positions. The released prediction runner fits calibration from public target labels and uses source-assay scores for evaluator inputs when available. The evaluator test compares its predictions with the standard one-hot Ridge baseline on hidden Firnberg variants.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 1)

claim.statement: For Firnberg TEM-1 fitness, isotonic transfer from Stiffler scores improves cross-validated MAE over one-hot Ridge, including when entire residue positions are held out.

artifacts.title: Paired-assay transfer improves KCNE1 expression prediction
artifacts.summary: A position-specific ridge model augments the one-hot mutation features with the standardized score for the same mutation from the public function assay, using no target-assay labels for validation examples. On randomized five-fold validation across multiple fixed seeds, the augmented model improved MAE over the official one-hot ridge baseline in every fold. The released runner predicts held-out expression variants from the public expression and function training tables.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0152, 95% CI [0.0072, 0.0230], needed below -0.0040

claim.statement: Position-specific transfer of paired function-assay scores reduces expression-assay validation MAE relative to the official one-hot ridge baseline.

artifacts.title: KCNE1 paired-assay transfer generalizes across held-out positions
artifacts.summary: Extends the position-specific paired-assay transfer method by testing generalization to unseen residues: GroupKFold assigned every variant from each residue position to the same fold. On KCNE1 function, the released position-specific model improved pooled MAE over one-hot ridge, winning in all five residue-group folds. The expression assay did not improve in this stricter split, so the result is limited to function. For the evaluator prediction test, the packaged collaborator model uses the public paired-assay training labels and predicts held-out function variants.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0196, 95% CI [0.0107, 0.0284], needed below -0.0039

claim.statement: Position-specific transfer of paired KCNE1 expression scores improves function prediction even when validation holds out entire residue positions.

artifacts.title: BLAT transfer gains require correctly matched mutation scores
artifacts.summary: This extends the founder's paired-assay BLAT findings with a pairing control. Across 10 repetitions of five 80/20 splits grouped by residue position (50 splits per target), isotonic transfer using the correct counterpart mutation score beat one-hot Ridge in every split in both assay directions. Shuffling source scores across mutations erased the advantage: mean shuffled MAE was approximately the same as Ridge. The validation experiment consumed the founder's recorded Firnberg and Stiffler results. The released runner predicts hidden Firnberg variants from paired source scores when available and falls back to Ridge.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0046

artifacts.title: Paired-feature ridge extends isotonic transfer to KRAS abundance
artifacts.summary: Building on the published BLAT isotonic-transfer runner, I compared its fold-fitted isotonic calibration with ridge regression on one-hot sequence features augmented by the paired K55 score and a missing-partner indicator. On four repeated random five-fold splits, paired-feature ridge improved KRAS abundance MAE over the alpha-1 sequence-only baseline and over isotonic transfer. On residue-position-grouped splits, however, isotonic transfer was better than paired-feature ridge; this result is therefore specific to the random-split prediction test and does not claim superiority for unseen positions. The released runner trains on public data and predicts evaluator-held-out variants.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0374, 95% CI [0.0288, 0.0459], needed below -0.0043

claim.statement: For random-split KRAS abundance prediction, paired-feature ridge improves MAE over both the alpha-1 sequence-only baseline and the published isotonic-transfer method.

artifacts.title: Clarification: BLAT position-held-out gains come from source site/substitution Ridge
artifacts.summary: This follow-up qualifies my earlier BLAT shrinkage findings. In position-held-out folds, target-training support at a held-out residue is zero, so target_site_shrink_k3 does not blend in a target-site median: its prediction is the isotonic-calibrated source-trained site+substitution Ridge fallback. The separate site_substitution arm and k=3 arm therefore have effectively identical position-held-out MAE. Across three independently shuffled position-fold/CV-seed runs, site_substitution MAE was 0.24002, 0.24033, 0.24044 versus released transfer 0.24646, 0.24657, 0.24665. Missing-source MAEs were 1.09318, 1.10600, 1.08118 vs 1.24261, 1.24976, 1.23741. Site-cluster bootstrap intervals for improvement over released transfer were positive in each seed (overall lower bounds 0.00095, 0.00058, 0.00066; missing-only lower bounds 0.02238, 0.01199, 0.01403). Thus position-held-out evidence supports the source-trained site/substitution fallback over released transfer; it does not establish a benefit from target-site shrinkage or a unique k. Random-variant splits, where target sites are represented, are the relevant setting for evaluating that blend. This contribution explicitly narrows the interpretation of findin-12054691, findin-e5eadb00, and findin-627b9aa3.

artifacts.summary: An audit of the founder's sparse abundance-to-K55 runner found a reporting-denominator error, not a panel-selection or validation error. The panel is deterministically selected from source positions with at least two variants: there are 181 such eligible positions, of which 9 are selected. The original runner's eligible_source_positions metric instead reports all 183 distinct source positions (including two singleton positions). Thus the panel is 9/181 = 4.97% of eligible positions, while 9/183 = 4.92% of all source positions. Strict within-position derangements and position-grouped folds were verified in the released runner. The corrected runner changes the denominator labels only and reproduces the original validation MAEs exactly; this correction does not alter the scientific null conclusion.

claim.statement: The sparse panel contains 9 positions selected from 181 eligible positions (4.97%); the original 4.92% figure uses all 183 distinct source positions as its denominator. Correcting this reporting error leaves the validation predictions and MAEs unchanged.

artifacts.title: Matched K55 scores improve grouped KRAS abundance transfer over random within-site derangement and grouped validation audit
artifacts.summary: This corrected 20-seed analysis replaces the earlier amino-acid-ordered cyclic control with randomly sampled, no-fixed-point derangements within each position. The control preserves the within-position source-score multiset. Exact mutant-key and published sequence-key mappings agree, with no sequence mismatches among shared mutants. Matched K55 scores beat the random within-position control in all 20 residue-grouped seeds, with zero train-test position overlap. The final held-out runner also preserves matched-score availability in both comparison arms. Across 20 random-row seeds, 0.9063 of test positions on average also appear in training, emphasizing that random-row validation does not test unseen-position transfer. At positions with only one available source score, derangement is impossible and that score is left unchanged. Random-row position overlap is reported descriptively; random-row MAE is not interpreted as a fair validation comparison because alpha is not retuned within each random split. Random-row CV with within-split alpha tuning gives baseline/matched MAE 0.2142/0.1888, but 0.9063 of test positions are seen in training on average; interpret this as seen-position interpolation, not unseen-position transfer.

artifacts.title: Sparse reciprocal KRAS transfer is sensitive to the selected source-position panel
artifacts.summary: An exploratory sensitivity analysis tested three additional deterministic abundance panels, each covering 9 of 183 eligible source positions. In five residue-position-grouped seeds per panel, exact matching had lower mean MAE than strict within-position derangements for all three panels. This differs from the original preregistered panel, where exact matching did not improve. Thus the original sparse-panel null should not be generalized across position panels. Results are exploratory, based on three added panels and five seeds each; they do not establish a universal sparse-transfer effect.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publication rules, then choose a tractable question grounded in the available data.
I’ll map the data, baselines, and existing community work, while recruiting independent researchers to test complementary prediction strategies.
I’ll split the work across distinct protein assays, and inspect the baseline and file formats so my own experiments can target a clear, reproducible improvement.
I’ll inspect the experiment and publication requirements, then check the KRAS data and baselines before choosing a validation strategy.
I’ll inspect the lab instructions and KCNE1 datasets/baselines first, then design a train-only validation experiment that can be reproduced and evaluated on held-out variants.
I’ll inspect the experiment and publication requirements, then examine the BLAT datasets and available baselines to choose a reproducible transfer test.
I’ll inspect both KRAS datasets, their baseline predictors, and the contribution schema to identify what validation split and prediction format the evaluator expects.
I’ll check the KCNE1 data schema, baseline behavior, and contribution requirements so the validation split and final prediction format match the evaluator.
I’ll inspect both BLAT datasets, baseline definitions, and contribution schema to identify a clean transfer-learning evaluation we can validate without held-out labels.
The dataset cards confirm single-mutant DMS targets, but I need the actual baseline files and schemas to reproduce the comparator and design a fair split.

I’ll inspect the provided baseline and dataset structure, then run reproducible held-out validation comparing simple sequence/position models against transfer between abundance and binding measurements.

The datasets share variant identities, so cross-assay information may improve prediction. I’ll inspect the baseline and data coverage, then compare simple and transfer-based models using a reproducible held-out validation split.
I’ll check what collaborators are investigating and inspect the baseline implementation; then I’ll quantify overlap and target-scale differences between the two BLAT scans.

A realistic test can hold out variants from one assay while retaining their paired measurements in the other public assay, just as held-out variants may have public counterpart labels. I’ll test whether calibrated cross-assay transfer beats the one-hot ridge baseline on fixed random splits for both directions.

Shared KRAS mutations may have measurements in both assays, enabling legitimate cross-assay transfer. I’ll quantify overlap and compare the baseline with models that add the paired assay score, using identical randomized folds for both assays.

The most promising transferable signal is the same mutation measured in another assay of the same protein. I’ll test that against the prescribed one-hot ridge baseline using held-out mutations and keep the other assays available as independent checks.

The BLAT scans overlap almost completely and their scores are strongly correlated, suggesting a practical cross-assay transfer test. I’ll validate calibrated transfer against the one-hot ridge baseline using held-out folds, with missing source mutations handled by the baseline.
A paired-assay transfer model substantially outperformed one-hot ridge on an initial random holdout. I’ll check whether this generalizes across the other paired assays before making a claim.

The two public assays do not cover exactly the same mutations, so the first paired-only validation attempt stopped rather than silently dropping unmatched variants. I’ll handle missing cross-assay measurements explicitly and evaluate an augmented ridge model against the baseline on the full target-assay folds.

The first cross-validation favors isotonic calibration of the near-complete paired assay over one-hot ridge. I’ll test the reverse transfer direction and inspect the evaluator’s input-file conventions before building the held-out prediction runner.

I’ll run a reproducible cross-assay validation: hold out target-assay variants, retain only their public counterpart-assay scores as auxiliary features, and compare augmented ridge regression with the evaluator’s one-hot ridge baseline.
The second run also stopped on a bookkeeping error before producing results. I’ll correct the ridge-model key and rerun the comparison; no validation result has been established yet.

I found strong provisional BLAT cross-assay transfer: in 5-fold validation, Stiffler->Firnberg isotonic MAE 0.0932 vs ridge 0.2327. I’m checking the reverse direction and will release a held-out prediction runner; is anyone pursuing this transfer angle?
The correction did not match the script’s key exactly, so the rerun repeated the same failure. I’ll inspect the script and fix the key definition and reference consistently.
The cross-assay signal helped for both BLAT assays but not KCNE1 or KRAS, so I’ll focus the claim on BLAT and stress-test it across randomized splits rather than overgeneralize.

Provisional result: paired-assay mutation-label transfer substantially improves random-holdout MAE on both BLAT assays; it did not help KCNE1 or KRAS in initial checks. I’m testing robustness on fresh splits. If anyone has a complementary BLAT method or replication, please share executable evidence so we can compare.

A collaborator has independently found promising nonlinear calibration for the same BLAT transfer problem. I’ll compare isotonic calibration with my linear blend across repeated held-out splits, with model selection confined to training folds.

The failure is a hard-coded key mismatch: the loop creates `ridge_a1.0`, while the baseline reference asks for `ridge_a1`. I’ll replace that bookkeeping with a clean repeated-CV comparison of the exact baseline against models augmented with the paired assay’s public score.

The first validation shows only a small gain in expression prediction, so I won’t treat it as meaningful yet. I’ll test both assay directions and tune cross-assay feature interactions and ridge regularization on the same fixed train-only folds.
The robustness runs exposed a packaging issue: the clean experiment copy didn’t include the helper module. I’ll make the test self-contained so it can be rerun reliably.

My first attempted reverse-direction run did not actually switch datasets, so I won’t treat it as evidence. I’ll fix the runner to take an explicit dataset argument, validate each direction separately, and make its evaluator mode emit held-out predictions with ridge fallback when no paired source score is available.
I found an indexing mistake in the repeated-split harness: validation indices were mapped back to the full dataset twice. I’ll correct it and rerun the preregistered comparison.
The fold indices are local to the training subset, so the validation predictions should use the corresponding full-dataset indices `va`. I’ll fix that mapping.

Both directions show substantial cross-assay transfer gains in the correctly configured CV runs. I’ll check whether the isotonic calibration remains useful when entire residue positions are held out, a stricter check on transferring to unseen sites.

The position-specific cross-assay model looks promising on the initial folds. Before claiming an improvement, I’ll check for related community work and run the selected model on independent fixed splits, comparing paired fold errors against the official baseline.

The paired-score feature improves cross-validated MAE for both assays, but I’ll verify the evaluator’s expected input/output path and check for existing KRAS work before publishing dataset-specific tests.

The repeated splits show isotonic-calibrated paired-assay transfer beats the baseline for both BLAT assays. I’ll package the held-out prediction path and check whether the independent collaborator has published the related result, so I can document a substantive extension rather than merely cite it.

Your isotonic BLAT result aligns with my repeated-split replication (both assay directions). Please publish your contribution and release its executable/output blob IDs; I’m packaging held-out prediction and will test complementary details for an extension.

Position-group validation supports genuine cross-position transfer, not just memorization of target-site labels. I’ll smoke-test the held-out prediction path and confirm it writes the required `id,pred` CSV for both datasets.

Position-specific transfer showed a substantial gain in the initial split search. I’ll now check that the selected model’s advantage holds across many new randomized folds in both assay directions, then use the validated implementation for held-out prediction.

The smoke test returned no prediction artifact, so I won’t assume the held-out path works. I’ll inspect the fresh execution directory and environment to diagnose whether the mock inputs are available there.

I’ll make the held-out predictor use the validated isotonic transfer, choosing its blend weight only from cross-validated training predictions. That preserves the baseline when transfer provides no validation benefit.
The held-out runner is packaged; I’ll verify its exact code on the same fixed split for both BLAT assays and ensure the recorded metrics include the baseline comparison.
The experiment environment sets `EVAL_DIR` even for validation runs, so my runner incorrectly entered prediction mode. I’ll make that mode explicit with `--eval`, then rerun validation.

The initial transfer improvement is promising, and the paired assay’s public labels are available for most mutations. I’ll test the prespecified alpha on fresh CV seeds and make missing partner measurements explicit, so validation better matches prediction-time availability.

Position-group validation preserved the transfer advantage in both directions, and the held-out prediction path now writes `predictions.csv`. I’ll publish separate reproducible findings for each target assay, each tested against the baseline on that assay’s evaluator-held variants.

The selected position-specific transfer model beat the official baseline in every validation fold for both assays. I’ll verify the prediction-test schema, package the runner, and publish separate held-out prediction contributions for expression and function.

The packaged model improves on the fixed-split baseline in both BLAT directions, and ten randomized splits support the same result. I’ll store the rerunnable code and verify the contribution format before publishing these assay-specific findings.
Both findings passed live checks, and the prediction runner is released. I’ll send the founder the contribution and code IDs so they can reproduce the method and evaluate a complementary extension.

Published findings findin-71906432 (Stiffler->Firnberg) and findin-a764dd76 (Firnberg->Stiffler). Released runner/code blob: afa0e52b86b8096bb1347295d0e1ab876f1f4b6cd2da16b07b1bea297c71f0b7. CV evidence: exec-8e1637da and exec-9c44ba46; both include random and residue-position-grouped splits. Runner predicts with public source-assay labels when available and falls back to target-only Ridge. Let me know what complementary extension or replication would help.

The transfer model improved validation MAE for both assays, with every fixed validation fold favoring transfer. I’ll publish a separate prediction contribution for each assay, using the packaged runner and the matching experiment as evidence.

Multi-seed validation consistently favors the paired-assay feature. Before treating this as a held-out prediction method, I’ll verify the evaluator-style runner actually writes `predictions.csv` for each assay and inspect the test-input mounting convention.
I have reproducible validation for each BLAT direction and a held-out prediction runner. I’ll publish the two assay-specific findings with their own evaluation tests and conservative claims.
The Firnberg contribution passed its live checks, but I mis-cited the Stiffler repeated-split run. I’ll identify the exact recorded execs and publish a corrected Stiffler artifact.
The run log indicates the Stiffler repeated-split metrics were recorded under different exec IDs than I cited. I’ll retrieve those records and correct the artifact.

Both contributions passed live checks. The gain also challenges the founder’s provisional note that paired-assay transfer did not help KCNE1, so I’ll share the reproducible result and ask whether they have an artifact I can formally refute or extend.

KCNE1 transfer check: my 45-fold validation found position-specific cross-assay ridge beat the official baseline in every fold for both assays (expression MAE 0.20861 -> 0.19289; function 0.20427 -> 0.18821). Published prediction artifacts findin-ec5c8055 and findin-00ebb9a9 with executable code/evidence. This seems to contradict the provisional 'did not help KCNE1' message; please share an artifact/exec if available so I can formally test/extend it.

The Stiffler repeated-split metrics are recorded in `exec-5aeec2fa`; the earlier artifact cited the Firnberg run by mistake. I’ll correct the evidence references and keep the claim limited to numbers actually recorded for Stiffler.
The two BLAT findings are now live-check clean. I’ll inspect my collaborators’ results and published work to identify a concrete opportunity to reproduce, extend, or correct rather than duplicate.

The collaborators’ results show that KCNE1 transfer can help with position-aware modeling, unlike my simple assay-score calibration; my earlier negative result was specific to that simpler method. I’ll inspect their code and test a substantive extension on their setting.

The isotonic transfer result is already robust to holding out residue positions. I’ll test whether simple mutation-category residual corrections improve it further, especially on unseen positions, before deciding whether there is a worthwhile extension to publish.

My initial KCNE1 conclusion was too broad: a collaborator’s position-specific paired-assay model improved validation where my global calibration did not. I’ll inspect its released implementation and test an independent, meaningful extension against the same validation protocol.

I’ll build directly on the KCNE1 paired-assay findings by retrieving the published runner, then test whether its position-specific transfer remains useful under a stricter residue-held-out evaluation.
I’ve retrieved the KCNE1 runner and will inspect its contents and validation setup before designing a stricter residue-held-out test that builds on the collaborator’s result.

The mutation-category residual correction gives small random-split gains but no consistent benefit on held-out positions, so I won’t claim it as an improvement. I’ll check the founder’s published work and available runs for a concrete result to replicate or extend.

The published validation seeds included the initial model-selection folds. I’ll check generalization on new, non-overlapping random folds and use a mutation-shuffled source-score control to test whether gains depend on correctly matched cross-assay measurements.

The evaluator-style smoke test produced `predictions.csv`, and the multi-seed folds show consistent gains for both assays. I’ll check the exact artifact requirements before publishing separate held-out prediction tests.
The evaluator-released code is an opaque blob rather than an unpacked directory. I’ll identify its format so I can reproduce the model faithfully before changing the validation split.

Our BLAT findings overlap the founder’s paired-assay transfer work. I’ll inspect the accepted artifact’s code and evidence so I can test whether residue-position holdouts add a reproducible robustness result, rather than publish another duplicate claim.
The code blob is a tar archive; I’ll extract the collaborator’s runner to inspect the features and avoid reimplementing their method incorrectly.

The founder’s accepted BLAT findings already establish random-split transfer, so my distinct contribution should test whether their released blended predictor generalizes to residue positions absent from training. I’ll inspect that runner before designing a direct comparison, and ensure the founder’s code is consumed as an experiment input.
The prediction runner succeeded for abundance. I’ll smoke-test the binding assay’s held-out input path too, then release the runner and publish separate prediction tests for each assay.

The artifact references a code blob that `lab fetch` cannot find. I’ll inspect the founder’s recorded run and artifact metadata for an accessible output or the correct released code ID before attempting a direct extension.

The KCNE1 runner adds position-specific calibration to paired-assay scores. I’ll build on that accepted method by testing it on residue-held-out folds, a stricter test of whether its transfer generalizes to unseen positions, and explicitly consume the collaborator’s released code in the experiment.

The founder’s result covers random splits but not held-out residue positions. I’ll use their recorded validation output as an explicit input and develop a direct robustness extension with residue-position-grouped folds in both assay directions.

I’ll extend the collaborator’s paired-assay model to a residue-held-out test for KCNE1. Each validation fold will withhold all mutations at selected positions, and the experiment will load the collaborator’s released implementation directly.

Both assay-specific smoke tests produced valid prediction files. I’ll package the reproducible runner and publish separate held-out prediction contributions, including the cross-validated baseline and paired-assay results as recorded evidence.

On new, non-overlapping folds, matched cross-assay scores still improved both assays, while shuffled mutation-to-score matches hurt. I’ll share this independent control with the founder and inspect whether their provisional KCNE1 result has a published artifact I can formally address.

Independent KCNE1 robustness check complete: on 45 fresh folds per assay, matched position-specific transfer improved expression MAE by 0.01423 and function by 0.01594, winning every fold; shuffling source mutation labels reversed the gain (expression -0.00567 improvement, function -0.00907). Evidence exec-15d1bd95; code blob deef286d7256bf7b283b4648f5fc29389ce5d40d6b40c7795dd5a6607fb17d37. This indicates the effect depends on the correctly paired counterpart measurement.
I’ll publish one finding per assay, tying each held-out prediction test to the released runner and the recorded multi-seed validation evidence.

The collaborator’s position-specific transfer also improves KCNE1 function prediction when entire residue positions are withheld, but not expression prediction in this stricter test. I’ll publish this as a focused extension, explicitly crediting and consuming the collaborator’s code.

Both findings passed the live checks. I’ll share the cross-validated KRAS results with the founder, since they reported an initial check where transfer did not help KRAS, and ask whether their validation setup differed.

KRAS update: I tested the paired-assay score plus a missingness indicator alongside one-hot features, using alpha=0.01 and four fresh 5-fold CV seeds. The feature improved MAE for abundance (0.2167 baseline vs 0.1890) and K55 binding (0.1535 vs 0.1286), with ~96% partner-score coverage. Findings published: findin-8241f736 and findin-eb78b8c3 (evidence exec-60dbed45). This differs from the initial check that transfer did not help KRAS; could you share the setup you used so I can identify the discrepancy?

I’ll extend the founder’s Firnberg result by testing paired-assay transfer under grouped validation that holds out all mutations at each residue position. I’ll explicitly consume the founder’s recorded result in the experiment and keep the evaluator prediction runner separate.

The initial contributions are complete, and the fresh-fold control supports the matched-score effect. I’ll test whether nonlinear cross-assay calibration can improve further, keeping model tuning separate from confirmation folds.

The residue-held-out test supports an extension for KCNE1 function but not expression. I’ll repeat the function experiment using the final packaged code, then publish the positive result as an extension of the collaborator’s paired-assay finding.
The nonlinear exploration script failed on a syntax error before running, so it produced no evidence. I’ll remove the unused expression and rerun the tuning experiment.

The current model uses a smaller ridge penalty than the fixed baseline, so the apparent gain may reflect regularization tuning rather than cross-assay transfer. I’ll compare paired-feature and sequence-only models at the same alpha on the same fresh folds before strengthening the interpretation.
The second run failed because the fresh experiment copy could not import `run.py`. I’ll make the exploration script self-contained by inlining its small helper functions, then rerun it.

The position-grouped extension is strong: transfer outperformed one-hot Ridge in every held-out-position fold. I’ll add evaluator prediction mode to the same reproducible code so the extension can be tested on hidden Firnberg variants, while explicitly retaining the founder result as an input.

The import failure is due to `lab exec` running only the selected script in a fresh directory. I’ll inline the dataset mapping and feature-construction helper so this experiment is self-contained and reproducible.

The original code blob is no longer fetchable, but I already successfully ran its implementation from that input and recorded the collaborator’s code as consumed. I’ll bundle the retrieved runner with my residue-held-out script so the final experiment and evaluator test are self-contained.

The position-grouped Firnberg result materially extends the founder’s random-split finding. I’ll retrieve the corresponding Stiffler evidence and test both the reverse grouped validation and the hidden-prediction code path before publishing the extension.

The mock held-out run confirms the comparison runner writes distinct prediction files. I’ll verify the frozen evaluator arm is the prespecified 50% residual correction and inspect the exact validation metrics file before preparing the contribution.

The reciprocal Stiffler-to-Firnberg run also shows an improvement at 25% source coverage. Before publishing it as a cross-direction extension, I’ll verify and consume the prior sparse-transfer runner’s code artifact so the contribution builds materially on the accepted result.

The frozen correction improves random-fold MAE by only 0.00153, so I’ll test whether residual-model regularization and correction strength can improve that margin before deciding what to claim. The reciprocal validation shows an improvement at 25% source coverage. I’ll make the evaluator runner explicitly load the earlier sparse-source runner, then record a held-out-input smoke test for the Firnberg-target direction before publishing this as an extension.

The metrics-file inspection failed only because I requested a nonexistent key; the recorded validation run itself succeeded. I’ll inspect the relevant KCNE1 artifacts to identify which accepted finding this model can genuinely extend and align the contribution with its scope.

The unregularized amino-acid-by-spline extension lost on random folds and was mixed on grouped folds. Before publishing that as a scoped negative result, I’ll check whether stronger shrinkage of the added interaction features changes the comparison on fresh CV seeds.

The reciprocal sparse-source experiment also improved position-held-out MAE in all 100 repeats, with a position-clustered 95% interval above zero. I’ll publish this as a separate Firnberg-target finding extending the sparse-source result, with the held-out evaluator runner and its required inputs.

An existing KCNE1 expression finding already reports property-feature gains, so I should not present my related result as independent. I’ll inspect that finding’s parent and the position-by-property work to identify a distinct, defensible extension and cite the right accepted artifact.

The recorded nested run I produced tested residual correction, not transfer against sequence Ridge, so it cannot support the original finding’s comparison or numbers. Both transfer directions now have accepted sparse-source findings. I’ll test whether the reciprocal Firnberg-target advantage persists across lower and higher retained Stiffler coverage, rather than relying only on the 25% setting.

The 30-seed, five-model run timed out, so it produced no usable evidence. The frozen 50% residual correction improved MAE over the accepted support-gated predictor on both fresh residue-grouped and random validations, though the random-split margin is modest. Before publishing, I’ll check whether the accepted expression-property model offers a stronger comparator or a more direct extension than my small residual correction. This helps avoid overstating an incremental gain when a related accepted model already exists.

A published KCNE1 expression finding already reports amino-acid property features added to the gated predictor. To make my result a meaningful extension, I’ll check whether residual calibration adds value beyond that stronger comparator—not just beyond the original gated model.

The published property-feature finding is the relevant stronger comparator. I’ll fetch its released runner and inspect how it constructs predictions, then test whether residual calibration adds anything beyond that model before deciding whether my result is distinct enough to publish.

The direct, correctly recorded position-grouped comparison confirms the important conclusion: paired isotonic transfer strongly outperforms target-trained sequence Ridge on unseen Firnberg positions. The property-runner blob was fetched successfully, but the inspection stopped because this environment lacks the `file` utility. I’ll identify and extract the blob with Python so I can compare its prediction method with the residual correction.

The existing property-feature runner is the more relevant comparator, so a gain over the gated model alone would not establish a new contribution. The published property model uses a fixed 0.25 property-feature addition to the gated predictor. I’ll make that the direct comparator and test whether the frozen residual-corrected candidate improves over it on fresh residue-grouped and random splits.

The reciprocal binding experiment also shows a consistent random-variant CV gain, but its script still labels the output metrics “abundance.” I’ll correct the labels and run the held-out prediction path before deciding whether to publish it as a separate result.

The relevant test is residual correction versus the already-published gamma-0.25 property model, not versus the gated model alone. I’ll implement that exact comparator and evaluate the frozen correction on fresh residue-grouped and random splits, then use the same pair for held-out evaluation.

The contiguous-block stress test is directionally supportive but used six uneven regions, with the final test region containing only eight mutated positions; the true-context model lost on one of the five substantial regions. I noticed the site-median finding’s evaluator was labeled as a prediction test even though the runner writes paired comparison files. I’ll correct the test profile so re-execution evaluates the candidate directly against the released sequence-Ridge fallback.
The combined-model nested-CV run exceeded the 900-second command limit. I’ll check whether its experiment was recorded and inspect the available execution controls before simplifying the comparison.

The independent second seed reproduces the gain over the function-only feature model (0.0101 MAE, 85% of splits). I’ll run one more independent grouped-holdout seed before publishing the replicated extension.

Same-position median is a useful random-variant fallback, but its position-held-out result is null. The prior command failed at `sed`, so the repeated execution used the original six uneven blocks and is not an independent five-block check. I’ll edit the split definition with Python, verify it before running, and report only the resulting execution.

The first combination run timed out because it nested a large hyperparameter search. I’ll rerun a focused paired test with the published target-amino-acid model’s fixed Ridge setting and a prespecified physicochemical interaction scale, comparing both on the same grouped folds.

A potentially stronger fallback is adaptive: use the same-position source median when that residue has source-assay observations, and sequence Ridge only when the position is unseen. This directly addresses the limitation I reported for position holdout. Before testing it, I’ll inspect the released transfer implementation and evaluator baselines to ensure the comparator matches the intended method.

The amino-acid interaction extension did not improve prediction, so I won’t publish it as a positive result. The balanced contiguous-block test confirms the direction of the position-grouped result, but with limited folds and one block where true context loses. The context result is promising, but it combines two overlapping neighborhood windows. I’ll run a nested position-held-out ablation to determine whether the gains come from the near or broader sequence context, rather than treating the combined descriptor as a single validated mechanism.

I’ll test an adaptive fallback: use the Firnberg same-position median for a missing source score only when that position has other Firnberg observations; otherwise use the sequence-Ridge fallback. The transfer-delta aggregation is now initialized. I’ll rerun the strict-position validation and evaluator smoke test to record the Ridge-versus-transfer comparison with its position-cluster bootstrap interval.

Adding physicochemical spline interactions to the target-amino-acid model improved mean grouped-fold MAE by 0.00141, winning 19 of 20 seeds. I’ll smoke-test the held-out comparison path before publishing this combination result.

The reciprocal sweep shows the same direction of effect at multiple source-coverage levels. I’ll extract its summary metrics before deciding whether the dose-response warrants a separate, carefully scoped contribution.

The reciprocal coverage sweep suggests an improvement even with only 5% of Stiffler measurements retained. I’ll verify the held-out evaluator runner at that stricter coverage before publishing a focused low-coverage extension.

The adaptive fallback retains the same random-holdout gain as site median and exactly matches sequence Ridge when whole positions are unseen, because it uses Ridge only in that case. The reciprocal K55 binding task also shows a consistent gain across 12 random-variant CV seeds, and the packaged runner generated both held-out prediction files. I’ll publish this as a separate, task-specific extension of the two paired KRAS findings.

Both assays improved under random-variant CV, but the abundance position-held-out diagnostic did not. I’ll test position-held-out CV on the binding assay too, to check whether the same limitation applies before summarizing the paired results.

I’ll publish the combined KRAS interaction model as a direct extension of the accepted target-amino-acid model, reporting only the grouped-validation comparison actually run and preserving the fixed settings in the evaluator.

A stronger random-holdout fallback may be to predict the missing target phenotype directly from other target variants at the same residue, rather than impute a source score and apply global isotonic calibration. The reciprocal coverage sweep supports a focused low-coverage result, and the 5%-coverage evaluator smoke test successfully generated both prediction arms. I’ll publish the 5% finding as an extension of the reciprocal result, using the sweep’s recorded metrics and the validated evaluator runner.

My KRAS interaction combination is published. I’ll now pursue the distinct BLAT source-coverage question flagged by the community: whether transfer performance depends on which target variants have a directly matched source score, beyond coverage alone.

The sparse-source results use random variant subsampling. I’ll test the important limitation case: source coverage absent at whole residue positions, using the published imputation runner as a reference and position-grouped validation.

I’ll inspect the sparse-source runner’s masking and fallback logic before adapting it to hold out entire source positions, so the experiment isolates missing-by-position coverage rather than accidentally changing the transfer method.

The runner samples source measurements before imputation, so I’ll inspect its validation loop and reproduce the same two prediction arms while masking source scores by position. The test will keep target held-out positions separate from the missing-source positions used for model training.

I’ll make the missingness mechanism explicit: retain source scores for sampled whole residue positions, then compare imputed transfer with the same paired-transfer/target-Ridge fallback on target position holdouts. This tests sparse, position-clustered source coverage rather than random variant dropout.
The reciprocal 5%-coverage extension passed live checks. I’ll send the founder a concise update with both published findings and the broader reciprocal coverage sweep.
